new_statements.quote: Like in other Yolŋu languages, stress is found on the first syllable of a word. I refer to this as primary stress (marked by ˈ). In polysyllabic words there also seems to be a secondary (or minor) stress on the third or fourth syllable (marked by ֽ ). [...] Words with three syllables have also been found with secondary stress: ˈssֽs, e.g. /ˈwaɭ.mʊ.ֽɖa/ 'moon, month', /ˈbu.ku.ֽwɛj/ 'five' [...] Words with four syllables or more all bear both primary and secondary stress. The latter is either placed on the third or fourth syllable: ˈssֽss, e.g. /ˈga.ɽa.ֽn̪a.ɽa/ '(in order) to go/to come' [...] ˈsssֽs, e.g. /ˈbak.mi.ja.ֽma/ 'break', /ˈgʊ.rʊ.maʈ.ֽci/ 'magpie goose'
new_statements.citation: Kabisch-Lindenlaub, Juliane (2017). A grammatical description of Golpa, a dying Yolŋu language. Dr. phil. dissertation, Friedrich-Schiller-Universität Jena (disputation 21.06.2017). Section 3.4 'Stress'. [NOT on the works list; PDF was already in our check folder from the earlier reading; Golpa is the Yirritja-moiety sister variety of Yan-nhaŋu within Nhangu (yann1237; ISO lja)]

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog initial stress (initial stress) and refines it with a secondary stress on the third or fourth syllable. Caveat: describes Golpa, not the Yan-nhaŋu (Dhuwa/Yirritja Crocodile Islands) varieties, though the thesis states (p. 20) 'Stress patterns are similar to those found in other Yolŋu languages/varieties.'
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the first syllable of every word; words of three or more syllables may carry a secondary stress on the third or fourth syllable (three-syllable words: secondary on the third; four-plus-syllable words: always a secondary stress, on the third or the fourth syllable).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary (minor) stress on the third or fourth syllable; obligatory in words of four or more syllables, attested in some three-syllable words. Footnote 84 compares Gälpu (Wood 1978, 85f.): 1-3 syllable words primary only, 4-6 syllable words also secondary on third or fourth syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: English loans: either the stress moves to the native initial pattern (/baˈnana/ -> /ˈbinana/) or the English stress is kept, which can lead to loss of the initial unstressed syllable (/ˈna:p/ 'enough') (citing Schebeck 2001, 68); footnote 82 says the pattern is also reconstructed for proto-Australian (Dixon 1980, 469); stress in compounds and reduplications 'yet to be researched' (p. 58).
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog yann1237 'Nhangu' covers the Crocodile Islands Yan-nhaŋu clan varieties (six bäpurru varieties: Dhuwa Gamalaŋga, Gorryindi, Mäḻarra; Yirritja Bindarra, Ngurruwulu, Walamangu) and Golpa (ISO lja). Works 0-2 are about Yan-nhaŋu proper (Bowern's Milingimbi/Murruŋga documentation, speakers Baymarrwaŋa, Gularrbanga, Milinditj, Nyaŋbal, Nyuŋunyuŋu, Warrŋayun). The one source actually read (index 3) describes Golpa, the Yirritja-moiety Nhangu variety, and its statement is generalised by the author to Yolŋu varieties as a whole rather than checked on Yan-nhaŋu itself.
